exam: A 45‑year‑old man with HIV presents with confusion and asterixis – what immediate investigations and why? — Check electrolytes, BUN/creatinine, ABG; treat hyperkalaemia or acidosis first.
How would you differentiate uremic pericarditis from bacterial pericarditis? — Look for uremic signs, absence of fever, normal WCC; pericardial friction rub improves with dialysis.
What are the KDIGO criteria that define uremia? — eGFR <15 mL/min/1.73 m² or creatinine >5 mg/dL with systemic symptoms.
A patient cannot access dialysis; what temporising measures can you use? — Strict potassium restriction, sodium bicarbonate, careful fluid removal with diuretics if urine output present.
Why should NSAIDs be avoided in uremic patients? — They reduce renal perfusion and worsen toxin accumulation.
What reversible cause should be ruled out first in a patient with oliguria and rising creatinine? — Volume depletion/hypovolaemia; give isotonic fluids and reassess.
Explain the pathophysiology of uremic encephalopathy. — Accumulation of guanidine compounds and other neurotoxins depress neuronal activity, causing altered mental status.
When is emergent dialysis indicated in uremia? — Refractory hyperkalaemia, severe acidosis (pH <7.1), fluid overload unresponsive to diuretics, pericarditis, or encephalopathy.
ai.title: Uremia
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Uremia is the clinical syndrome of toxin accumulation due to severe renal failure. Recognise its systemic signs, identify reversible precipitants, and manage complications while arranging renal replacement.

b: Common in patients with diabetic nephropathy, hypertensive nephrosclerosis, HIV‑associated nephropathy, and post‑obstructive renal failure.
In low‑resource settings, delayed presentation and limited dialysis increase mortality.
sections.p: Uremia occurs when the kidneys can no longer excrete nitrogenous waste, leading to accumulation of urea, creatinine, and other toxins. It is a late manifestation of chronic kidney disease (CKD) or acute kidney injury (AKI).

b: Causes: prerenal (hypovolaemia, sepsis), intrinsic (glomerulonephritis, HIV‑related nephropathy, sickle‑cell nephropathy), post‑renal (obstructive uropathy, schistosomal fibrosis).
Life‑threatening complications: hyperkalaemia, metabolic acidosis, pericarditis, uremic encephalopathy, bleeding diathesis.
sections.p: Diagnosis rests on laboratory thresholds and systemic manifestations. Staging follows KDIGO CKD categories; uremia is usually CKD stage 5 (eGFR <15 mL/min/1.73 m²) or AKI with oliguria and rising creatinine.

b: Nausea, anorexia, pruritus, fatigue.
Neurologic: confusion, asterixis, seizures.
Cardiovascular: pericardial rub, hypotension, arrhythmias.
Dermatologic: uremic frost, pallor.
sections.p: Patients present with nonspecific symptoms that become systemic as toxins rise. Early recognition allows treatment of reversible causes and timely referral for dialysis.

t.b: How severe is renal dysfunction? Creatinine >5 mg/dL or eGFR <15 mL/min/1.73 m² indicates uremia.
Confirms nitrogenous waste accumulation; BUN >100 mg/dL supports uremia.
Detect hyperkalaemia, metabolic acidosis, and calcium‑phosphate imbalance.
Identify proteinuria, haematuria, or casts suggesting intrinsic disease.
Look for pulmonary oedema or pleural effusion from fluid overload.

b: Volume repletion for prerenal AKI; avoid nephrotoxins (NSAIDs, aminoglycosides).
Control hyperkalaemia: calcium gluconate (if ECG changes), insulin‑glucose, sodium bicarbonate; dialysis if >6.5 mmol/L or ECG changes.
Correct metabolic acidosis with sodium bicarbonate if pH <7.2 and symptomatic.
Treat uremic pericarditis with dialysis; give NSAIDs only if renal function improves.
Dialysis indications: refractory hyperkalaemia, severe acidosis, fluid overload, uremic encephalopathy, pericarditis.
sections.p: Treat underlying cause, correct metabolic derangements, and arrange renal replacement when indicated.
